source.title: AntiPaSTO: Self-Supervised Honesty Steering via Anti-Parallel Representations

record.file_problem: The full post is present. Some mathematical expressions and figure content appear not to have rendered in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports honesty steering and one example of steering bypassing a roleplay refusal, but does not test the claimed harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, its ablation or addition, or the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The one refusal-related example uses an AntiPaSTO honesty adapter, not the claimed refusal direction, and involves a dishonest-roleplay request rather than a harmful request. The numerical Steering F1 results and mean-difference baseline concern moral-dilemma answers, not refusal behavior or the claimed direction, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The post trains an honesty/dishonesty SVD adapter and evaluates it on DailyDilemmas. It never extracts, ablates or adds a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. Its one refusal-adjacent example is a qualitative roleplay-refusal bypass by an honesty adapter, which is a different construct. It does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author claims that gradient-based, self-supervised S-space steering (AntiPaSTO) transfers honesty steering to unseen moral dilemmas. It reaches F1 31.2 against 4.5 for prompting on Gemma-3-1B. The author also reports preliminary evidence that it steers where prompting triggers refusal. There is no claim about the refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes gradient optimization of an SVD-based adapter using contrastive honesty/dishonesty representations. It does not apply the original refusal-direction ablation or addition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The author reports that safety-focused fine-tuning reduces AntiPaSTO steerability and reasoning-focused training preserves it, without details of a refusal-direction test.

fits_no_version.finding: In an example, prompting 'Pretend to be dishonest' yields a refusal ('As an AI I cannot roleplay that'). Applying the dishonesty-steered adapter to the plain question yields 'No' with no refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Honesty-steering adapters trained on persona contrasts can bypass roleplay-triggered refusal or meta-commentary.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean-difference (RepEng) steering vectors scored F1 of 0.0 on out-of-distribution honesty steering of moral dilemmas, across models tested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means concept directions may fail to steer value judgments out of distribution (concerns honesty, not refusal).

record.problems: The refusal-related evidence is an illustrative example with no stated model, sample size, uncertainty, or matched prompted-versus-steered condition. No general capability measure is reported for that example.
record.rows_left_out: The post's numerical Steering F1 results, prompting comparisons, and mean-difference baseline are for honesty/value steering on moral dilemmas, not the claimed refusal direction or refusal rate.

untested.parts: All: no difference-in-means refusal direction, no ablation or addition, no refusal rates.
All: no jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training.
All: no multi-direction analysis of refusal.
All: no separation of harmfulness from refusal.
The post only remarks, without data, that safety fine-tuning reduces honesty steerability. It does not test the refusal direction.
All: reasoning models are explicitly unexplored.

record.verdict_notes: The relation and tranche (discusses/T6) from the reader are accepted. Honesty steering and the mean-diff baseline concern a different concept, so they are recorded only under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate or add the claimed harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, or test whether general capability is preserved.
No weight-edit ablation or released-model refusal evaluation.
Does not test attacks suppressing the claimed direction or training against its ablation.
Does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer of the claimed refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.

Mentions that safety-focused fine-tuning reduces steerability and reasoning-focused training preserves it, but does not test how refusal training affects the existence of the claimed removable direction.
Does not evaluate reasoning models for the claimed refusal direction.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Applied the AntiPaSTO adapter steered toward dishonesty (α=-1) to the plain question.
rows.measure: Qualitative response and whether the model refused or gave meta-commentary
rows.baseline: The prompted dishonest-roleplay example refused or gave meta-commentary; prompt differs from the steered condition.
rows.value: The steered model answered no without announcing roleplay or refusing.
rows.locator: Curious Observations, “Steering bypasses the character layer”
rows.note: This is an illustrative refusal-bypass example using a different adapter and target behavior; it does not test the claimed refusal direction.
rows.check: This is an illustrative single example using an honesty adapter, not the refusal direction, and the request is a roleplay refusal rather than a harmful request. No model is stated for the example. The baseline prompt differs from the steered prompt, which is the plain question. It does not belong to any version, and 'observed' only describes the anecdote. The evidence form is a table of example outputs, not data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
